text: Keeping a training run alive is only useful if the model that comes out is actually good. The cheapest signal to start with -- and one the training loop already produces almost for free -- is held-out loss and perplexity. This lesson covers what they measure, and just as importantly, what they don't.

Training loss shows how well the model fits the exact batches it optimized against. Held-out loss, computed on data the model never trained on, shows how well that fit generalizes. The two can diverge -- training loss keeps falling while held-out loss plateaus or rises, which is the signature of overfitting, and it's mechanically related to the catastrophic forgetting risk from earlier in this course.

Perplexity is just the exponential of the loss -- a model's average effective branching factor over the next token. Lower is better, and it's more legible than raw loss because small loss differences become larger, clearer perplexity differences. But perplexity measures exactly one thing: next-token prediction on a specific data distribution. It says nothing directly about instruction-following, reasoning, or safety.

Computing it is straightforward: run the model over held-out text with the input as both input and label, take the loss, and exponentiate it. Hugging Face's evaluate library packages this as a ready-made perplexity metric too, for quick comparisons across checkpoints without writing the loop by hand.

A model can have excellent perplexity on web text while being mediocre at following instructions, because those are different distributions. That's exactly why the rest of this chapter moves past perplexity -- starting next lesson with the standard benchmark suites, and where they fall short.
